opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question I get a lot, because there's this intuition that if the model just gets smart enough, all the scaffolding around it melts away. And I think that's half right. A lot of the clever prompting tricks and the brittle workarounds people wrote two years ago really have melted away, and that's good. But I'd separate that kind of glue code from what a harness actually does.

A harness is mostly the interface between the model and the world. It decides what the model can see, what it's allowed to touch, how state persists across a long task, how you recover when something fails halfway through, and how a human stays in the loop. None of those problems go away when the model gets smarter. If anything they get more important, because a more capable model gets handed longer, higher-stakes tasks. Once an agent is running for hours, editing real systems, spending real money, the questions around permissions, checkpointing, observability, and rollback become the whole game.

There's also a systems angle I keep coming back to. Think about operating systems: CPUs got enormously faster, and we didn't stop needing schedulers, memory isolation, or file systems. Faster compute actually made those abstractions more valuable, because you could do more with them. I think the harness is in a similar position. The model is the compute, and the harness is how you make that compute safe, composable, and useful inside an organization.

And then there's context management, which is underrated. Even with huge context windows, what you put in front of the model and when still matters a lot for quality, latency, and cost. Deciding what to retrieve, what to summarize, what to forget, and how to hand work between sub-agents is a design problem in its own right, and a better model doesn't solve it for you. It just rewards you more for getting it right.

So my bet is that the harness gets thinner in some places and thicker in others. The part that compensates for model weakness shrinks. The part that handles trust, state, and integration with the real world grows. That second part is where I think the durable value is.

r001.rationale: The response says a harness controls what the model can touch and handles permissions, but does not state that it enforces constraints instructions alone cannot reliably ensure.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I get this question a lot, and I think the honest version of the skeptic's argument is: the harness is scaffolding, scaffolding is a temporary workaround for model weakness, and once the model is smart enough the scaffolding goes away. And some of it does! A lot of the prompt-chaining tricks from 2023 are dead. Nobody misses them.

But I think that framing confuses two different things. There's the part of the harness that's compensating for the model being dumb, and there's the part of the harness that's defining what the model is even allowed to do and what it gets to see. The first part shrinks as models improve. The second part doesn't, because it's not about intelligence at all. It's about the environment.

Think about it from the model's side. Even a perfect model only acts through what you expose to it. What tools exist, how they're described, what the permission boundaries are, what gets fed back when a tool fails, how much of the world shows up in the context window and in what order. A smarter model makes better decisions over that surface, but it doesn't get to invent the surface. That's the harness. And the choices there are product choices and safety choices, not capability choices. You don't want a model that can run rm -rf on prod just because it's clever enough to know when it's appropriate. You want a system where that action requires a human, full stop, and the model being smarter doesn't change that.

The second thing is that the harness is where state lives. The model is stateless between calls. Memory, long-running task continuity, what happened three sessions ago, the fact that the user said never touch this directory again. Someone has to persist that and decide when it gets surfaced. Better models are better at using memory, but they're not the thing storing it.

And then the third piece, which I think people underrate, is that as models get more capable, the harness gets more important for verification, not less. When the model was weak, you could sort of eyeball its output. When it's running for an hour across forty tool calls, you need the harness to be your observability layer. What did it actually run, what came back, where did it diverge from the plan. That's a systems problem. It's the same reason we still have test suites and CI even though engineers got better over the last twenty years. We didn't throw out the infrastructure around human engineers because they improved. We built more of it.

So my short answer is: the parts of the harness that exist because the model is stupid will go away, and good riddance. The parts that exist because you're deploying an actor into a real environment with real consequences are going to grow, because the better the actor, the more you let it do, and the more you let it do, the more the surrounding system matters.

r001.rationale: The response says the harness defines what the model is allowed to do, including permission boundaries, and gives the example that a dangerous production action should require a human regardless of the model’s judgment. This communicates enforceable behavioral constraints beyond relying on the model alone.

astra-6.text:
I think better models change what you put in the harness, but they don’t eliminate the need for one. Some of what we build today is compensating for model weaknesses, and you should expect that stuff to go away. But some of it is managing the environment the model operates in: what tools it can use, what state persists, what it has permission to do, and how you know whether it succeeded.

Even a very capable model needs those things. If you give it a task that takes hours, you still need to handle interruptions, recover from failures, and get the right information into context. A better model might be better at deciding how to recover, but there still needs to be a system that makes recovery possible.

So I’d distinguish between scaffolding that helps a model reason and infrastructure that lets it act reliably. I expect the first category to keep shrinking and changing. The second becomes more valuable as we trust models with more consequential work.

r001.rationale: The response says a harness manages tools, permissions, and reliable action, but does not state that it enforces constraints that model instructions alone cannot reliably ensure.

sol-6.1.text:
I think better models change what you want in a harness, but they don’t eliminate the need for one. The model still operates inside a system: something has to give it access to tools, manage state, define permissions, and help it recover when something goes wrong.

Some of today’s scaffolding probably will disappear. If you’re compensating for a model’s inability to follow instructions or plan reliably, you should expect that code to become obsolete. But the architectural questions remain: What context does the model need? How do you know it succeeded? When should it ask a human?

And as models get more capable, we’ll ask them to do longer, more consequential tasks. That makes the surrounding system more important. The value shifts from helping the model produce a good answer to helping it reliably complete useful work.

r001.rationale: The response says the harness manages permissions and that models may not follow instructions reliably, but it does not clearly state that the harness can enforce behavioral constraints that instructions alone cannot ensure.
